text: A stack trace shows where the exception was created rather than where it was thrown. Why does that distinction exist at all?
choices: `throw` is compiled to a jump, which leaves no record, so only construction can be observed.
The trace is captured by the constructor walking the live frames, so reusing an exception object gives a stale trace.
The JVM records creation sites for garbage-collection purposes and reuses that data.
Java records the throw site too, but prints the creation site because it is more useful.
explanation: It matters in practice because the stack-trace-suppression trick — a pre-allocated exception whose `fillInStackTrace` does nothing — relies on it, and because the capture is where the cost lives: one million throws took 355 ms with a trace and effectively nothing without one.
